articles.title: Citi Prices Largest Single Bank-Contributed, Multi-Only CMBS Conduit Deal Since GFC
articles.narrative: Citigroup has priced the largest multifamily-only conduit CMBS transaction originated by a single bank since the Global Financial Crisis, totaling $816.9 million. The Citigroup Commercial Mortgage Trust 2026-MFAM1 comprises 27 five-year, interest-only loans on 27 multifamily properties, with all loans contributed by Citi Real Estate Funding. The deal's AAA bonds priced at swaps plus 80 basis points, tighter than a comparable multifamily CMBS transaction in May, reflecting strong market appetite for medium- to high-leverage loans on quality multifamily assets. The transaction offers geographic and sponsor diversification across core markets, including New York, Los Angeles, and Florida, appealing to bond buyers seeking diversification in a market dominated by single-asset, single-borrower deals.

data_points.notable_features: Comprises 27 five-year, interest-only loans on 27 properties; geographically diverse across core markets including New York, Los Angeles, and Florida.
data_points.project_notes: Largest multifamily-only conduit CMBS transaction originated by a single bank since the Global Financial Crisis; largest loan contribution in a conduit deal by a single bank post-Covid.

articles.title: South Florida Retail Markets Show Sub-5% Vacancy
articles.market: Miami / Fort Lauderdale / West Palm Beach, FL
articles.narrative: South Florida's retail sector is demonstrating strong performance, with low vacancy rates, resilient rental growth, and robust leasing and investment sales activity across Miami-Dade, Broward, and Palm Beach counties. Miami-Dade County leads with the lowest vacancy rate at 3 percent and rising asking rents, while Palm Beach County also saw positive absorption and rent increases. Broward County experienced a slight increase in vacancy and a decline in asking rents, though it still recorded significant leasing activity. The overall market performance indicates a healthy retail environment, defying earlier concerns about the sector's post-pandemic outlook.

articles.title: Prologis Beats Expectations With Record Leasing and Data Center Growth
articles.narrative: Prologis, the world's largest warehouse landlord, reported strong second-quarter 2026 earnings, exceeding expectations with record leasing activity and significant growth in its data center development pipeline. The company commenced $1.6 billion in new projects and acquired $1.8 billion in new real estate during the quarter. Notably, year-to-date data center starts, totaling $4 billion, have already surpassed full-year guidance, including an $800 million, 260-megawatt build-to-suit data center campus, which Prologis plans to sell upon completion. The REIT's CEO highlighted the strategic advantage of leveraging existing land, customer relationships, and operating capabilities to expand into data center and energy businesses, despite acknowledging growing challenges with approvals and entitlements for data center projects.
articles.market_intelligence: The U.S. industrial market is expected to see demand outrunning supply in 2026, with net absorption projected to approach 220 million square feet against 195 million square feet of completed developments. The European market recovery has been underway for nearly 12 months, with vacancy rates at 5.2%.

articles.title: Live Shopping Marketplace Storefront Takes 5K SF at 555 West 25th Street
articles.narrative: Storefront, a rapidly expanding e-commerce platform and live shopping marketplace, has secured a 4,700-square-foot office lease at 555 West 25th Street in Chelsea. The two-year agreement, with asking rents in the high $30s per square foot, was facilitated by Current Real Estate Advisors, which represented both the landlord and the tenant. The new space is expected to launch this fall, with the tenant anticipating future expansion within the building due to its fast growth.

The company, which develops AI software for finance and biotech, is relocating its commercial and customer teams to the boutique office building. data_points.notable_features: Located one mile from the junction of I-75 and I-275, offering 154 private patient rooms.

The company originally acquired the property in 2019 for $103 million through a Delaware statutory trust program, providing its 115 exchange investors with a 137 percent total return over a seven-year hold period. The sale generated over $17.5 million in distributions for the trust's investors.

articles.narrative: Marcus & Millichap has facilitated the sale of Commerce Centre, a 33,744-square-foot retail center in Prairieville, Louisiana. An East Coast-based investor acquired the property from a local owner at the full asking price, though the specific sale price was not disclosed. The center was 72 percent occupied at the time of the transaction.

articles.title: Partnership Sells 49,650 SF Industrial Complex in Carrollton, Texas
articles.narrative: A partnership between Birtcher Anderson & Davis Associates and Belay Investment Group has sold a 49,650-square-foot industrial complex in Carrollton, Texas. The two-building property was fully leased at the time of sale. The buyer and sales price were not disclosed.

articles.title: CRE Future Leaders: Draper and Kramer’s Lacy Guice
articles.narrative: This article profiles Lacy Guice, a leasing specialist at Draper and Kramer, highlighting her career trajectory and impact in the commercial real estate industry. Guice, a recipient of the Multi-Housing News Excellence Award for Leasing Professional of the Year in 2025, transitioned into property management after a career in live sound and production. She emphasizes the importance of community, problem-solving, and teamwork in her role, and expresses a desire for continued professional growth and leadership development within the industry.

articles.title: A varied economy? It’s the secret to success of Lansing’s CRE market
articles.narrative: Lansing, Michigan's commercial real estate market is demonstrating resilience due to its diversified economy, despite some sectors experiencing a slight slowdown, according to a new report from Colliers. The region's strong economic fundamentals, including its ranking among the top U.S. mid-sized metros for economic growth and workforce education, are supporting demand across industrial, office, and retail sectors. While industrial and office markets show increased vacancy and negative absorption, retail and multifamily sectors remain healthy with stable occupancy and rising rents, indicating a balanced but selective market for tenants and investors.
articles.market_intelligence: Greater Lansing ranks among the top 10 U.S. mid-sized metros for economic growth and among the top 15 regions nationally for workforce education levels. Industrial vacancy rates remain below the national average. Industrial rental rates increased from $7.28/SF at the end of 2025 to $7.52/SF in H1 2026. Office asking rents held steady at $17.04/SF despite elevated vacancies. Retail asking rents increased to $13.84/SF.

articles.title: Bradford Allen closes pair of leases with Illinois Retina in Chicago market
articles.narrative: Illinois Retina, a medical services provider, has executed two long-term leases in the Chicago metropolitan area. The company renewed and expanded its presence at Concourse Office Plaza in Skokie, Illinois, taking 16,228 square feet, and relocated to a new 8,728-square-foot facility at 9200 Calumet Ave. in Munster, Indiana. These transactions represent a continued commitment to serving patients across the region, with the Skokie lease marking a significant expansion from its previous footprint.

data_points.notable_features: The Skokie property comprises two 12-story medical office buildings, located 1 mile from the Edens Expressway. The Munster property is a single-story medical office complex located less than 2 miles from the Borman Expressway.
data_points.project_notes: The Skokie transaction represented a renewal and expansion from approximately 3,000 square feet. The Munster location relocated from a smaller facility.

articles.narrative: My Block, My Hood, My City (M3) hosted its Fourth Annual Downtown Day in Chicago, welcoming up to 1,300 youth and families from the city's South and West sides to experience cultural, educational, and recreational opportunities in the Loop. The event, supported by Museum of Illusions and Loop Dreams, a community initiative of 25 E. Washington, aims to connect young people with downtown Chicago and highlight the positive role businesses play in creating an inclusive urban experience. Participants received a $50 prepaid debit card to explore various categories, demonstrating a collaborative effort between businesses, nonprofits, and families to strengthen community ties.

articles.title: Lincoln Property acquires Spectrum Companies in Carolinas expansion
articles.narrative: Lincoln Property Company has acquired Charlotte-based developer The Spectrum Companies for an undisclosed sum, integrating Spectrum's operations into its Carolinas division. This strategic acquisition aims to accelerate development activities and facilitate further property acquisitions, particularly leveraging Spectrum's expertise in multifamily residential projects. The move is expected to be seamless due to the companies' shared vision and the existing relationship between their leadership.

articles.title: Brookfield-backed CSquare’s IPO missed target by $300M
articles.narrative: CSquare, a data center firm backed by Brookfield, completed its initial public offering, raising $1.05 billion by selling 50 million shares at $21 each. This amount fell $300 million short of its initial target, valuing the company at approximately $3.25 billion. The proceeds from the IPO are intended to repay a $771 million revolving credit facility and a $75 million promissory note held by Brookfield, which is expected to retain voting control post-offering. The company, formed last year through the merger of Cyxtera Technologies and Evoque Data Center Solutions, operates over 60 data centers across the U.S., Canada, and the U.K.

data_points.project_notes: CSquare was formed last year after Brookfield Infrastructure Partners acquired Cyxtera Technologies for $775 million and merged it with Evoque Data Center Solutions.

articles.market_intelligence: The IPO market for AI and data center infrastructure is active, with recent listings including SK Hynix's $26.5 billion U.S. listing, AI chipmaker Cerebras Systems' $6.38 billion listing, and Blackstone's data-center acquisition vehicle raising $2 billion. Blackstone Digital Infrastructure Trust also filed for an IPO, projecting to raise $1.75 billion to fund acquisitions of new construction data centers for hyperscalers.

articles.title: Industrial firms clear away glut of big-box warehouses
articles.narrative: The U.S. industrial market is experiencing a rapid absorption of large-format warehouses, reversing a pandemic-era glut. This surge in demand, driven by companies seeking to stockpile supplies amid geopolitical tensions and a push for domestic manufacturing, has led to a significant drop in vacancy rates for big-box facilities. As a result, landlords have regained pricing power, with rent escalations for large renewals more than doubling the pace of smaller spaces. Third-party logistics firms and data center support vendors are key drivers of this increased leasing activity, which has reached levels not seen since mid-2022.
articles.market_intelligence: Vacancy for warehouses 750,000 square feet or bigger fell to 7.3 percent in the first quarter, from 8.3 percent a year earlier. Meanwhile, vacancy for industrial buildings between 200,000 square feet and 500,000 square feet rose to 10.9 percent, up slightly from the prior year. Total industrial leasing hit 490 million square feet in the first six months of the year, up 27 percent from 2025. The overall U.S. vacancy rate was flat year over year at 8.2 percent in June. Lease escalations for renewals on spaces 500,000 square feet or larger averaged 84 percent in the first quarter. The average Class-A lease size, at 210,000 square feet, rose in the first three months of the year to its highest point since 2022, and 16.5 percent higher than in 2019.

articles.title: David Zaslav seeks to buy Camp Mohawk for $68M
articles.narrative: David Zaslav, CEO of Warner Bros. Discovery, through his Grandview Ventures, has made a $68 million stalking horse bid to acquire Camp Mohawk in White Plains, NY. The summer camp's parent company, Simad Holdings, filed for bankruptcy in June after defaulting on payments to Israeli bondholders and facing allegations of diverted funds. Zaslav's bid sets a floor price for the property, which was appraised at $85.8 million in December 2025, with other bidders able to submit higher offers in an upcoming auction. The acquisition is described as a personal family investment for Zaslav, whose children previously attended the camp.

The buyer secured $35 million in financing to execute its business plan, which includes leasing the substantial vacant space within the building.

articles.title: Jed Walentas, Tom Brady’s ex-manager abruptly settle legal battle over Bahamas mansion
articles.narrative: A legal dispute between Jed Walentas, CEO of Two Trees Management, and Will McDonough, Tom Brady's former manager, over a hurricane-damaged luxury rental property in the Bahamas has been abruptly settled. Walentas had been attempting to collect a $300,000 arbitration award from McDonough, who allegedly refused to pay his share of repair costs for the jointly developed mansion. The settlement was reached shortly after a Manhattan Supreme Court Justice authorized Walentas to serve McDonough via email, marking a resolution to the year-long collection effort.

data_points.notable_features: Luxury rental property located in the ultra-exclusive Bakers Bay resort.

articles.title: Arbor accused of dangling refinance before foreclosing on Georgia apartments
articles.narrative: The former owners of Chelsea Gardens Apartments in College Park, GA, have filed a lawsuit against Arbor Realty Trust, alleging that the lender engaged in a deceptive scheme. The lawsuit claims Arbor provided a high-interest bridge loan with the promise of Fannie Mae refinancing, but then deliberately stalled the refinancing process by demanding extensive repairs and ultimately foreclosed on the 474-unit multifamily property. An Arbor affiliate subsequently acquired the complex for $40 million at a foreclosure auction, leading the former owners to seek $175 million in damages.

data_points.project_notes: Property was previously acquired in 2022 for nearly $45 million with a $37.1 million bridge loan from an Arbor affiliate. The owners claim to have invested over $4 million in renovations and increased occupancy from 50% to 90% prior to the alleged scheme.

articles.title: Ralph Zucker’s luxury condo development in Asbury Park snags $186M loan

The financing, arranged by Meridian Capital Group, will fund the vertical development of the 112-unit beachfront property, which will also include ground-floor retail and extensive amenities. The project is notable for a penthouse unit that previously set a state record for the most expensive condominium sale.

articles.title: Faena Residences developers presell $30M penthouse for record price along Miami River
articles.narrative: A joint venture between KAR Properties and Fortune International Group has presold a penthouse unit at their Faena Residences luxury condominium development along the Miami River for $30 million. This presale sets a new record for the area in terms of both total price and price per square foot. The duplex penthouse, located in the east tower, will feature extensive interior and outdoor living spaces, including a private rooftop pool, wellness area, and entertainment spaces.

articles.title: “Animal House”: Brickell condo owners outraged by short-term rental goons
articles.narrative: This article details the transformation of The Club at Brickell Bay, a 43-story, 643-unit condominium in Miami, into a hub for short-term vacation rentals, leading to significant quality-of-life issues for permanent residents. The building's management and homeowner association board, none of whom reside in the building, are accused of lax enforcement of rules and city ordinances, including Miami's ban on short-term rentals in multifamily residential units. Residents report a range of illicit activities and a decline in living conditions, while investors are drawn to the high profitability of short-term rentals, which can generate up to $50,000 per unit annually. The situation highlights the broader 'Airbnb Effect' where investor profits from short-term rentals clash with residential quality of life and contribute to housing affordability challenges.

data_points.notable_features: 43-story residential condominium.
data_points.project_notes: Building management has been accused of running the condo like a hotel, with numerous violations and misconduct. A recent board election was marred by allegations of forged ballots and vote rigging.

articles.title: NFL’s Larry Ogunjobi turns developer with $16M spec home in Biscayne Point

The 4,300-square-foot property, dubbed "Glasshouse," is listed for $15.9 million. Ogunjobi acquired the site in 2024 for $4.6 million and developed the home through his platform, First of Many, aiming to capitalize on Miami's strong demand for move-in ready luxury residences.

articles.title: Firms tied to Argentine soccer money probe bought four Miami-Dade properties
articles.narrative: An FBI investigation into unusual financial transactions involving the Argentine Football Association (AFA) has revealed that a South Florida couple, Javier Faroni and Erica Gillette, purchased four properties in Miami-Dade County totaling $11 million. The couple's company, TourProdEnter, which served as the AFA's commercial agent, routed millions of dollars in AFA revenue to other Miami-Dade firms, some of which are believed to be shell companies. The property purchases, made between 2022 and 2025 through LLCs controlled by Faroni and Gillette, appear to have been all-cash transactions, raising questions about the beneficial owners and the source of funds.

articles.title: $1M rent, $100 steaks: Inside Coconut Grove’s booming restaurant scene
articles.narrative: Coconut Grove, once a bohemian enclave, has transformed into a premier dining destination in Miami, driven by a surge in retail rents. Average direct asking retail rents in the second quarter exceeded $110 per square foot, more than double the rates from a decade ago. This rapid appreciation has created a challenging environment for independent restaurateurs, with some being priced out, while also enabling landlords to curate a high-end tenant mix due to limited inventory and affluent clientele. The market's strong demand and limited supply are expected to sustain high rents, with no correction anticipated.

articles.title: Chicago’s top construction permits: Week ending July 17, 2026
articles.narrative: Onni Group secured a permit for a $190 million, 46-story residential tower at 931 North Halsted Street in Chicago's Near North Side. The project will feature 464 units, including 81 affordable units, along with extensive amenities. Additionally, Lathrop Preservation Phase IC obtained permits for an $85 million multi-building restoration of the historic Lathrop Homes, involving interior and structural alterations to six residential buildings. Amylu Foods LLC also filed plans for a $39.5 million commercial alteration at 1400 West 44th Street to expand a food manufacturing facility.

data_points.notable_features: 46-story tower with an exterior amenity deck, a sixth-floor pool, and 209 parking spaces; includes 81 affordable units.

articles.title: Shenouda’s Honore snags 70 East Lake for $9M with apartment conversion plans in mind
articles.narrative: Honore Properties has acquired the 17-story office building at 70 East Lake Street in Chicago for $9.2 million, with plans to convert it into approximately 170 apartments. The developer intends to invest around $40 million into the conversion of the nearly century-old building, which was 63% leased at the time of sale. This acquisition aligns with a broader trend of office-to-residential conversions in the Chicagoland area, aimed at addressing underutilized office space and increasing housing supply.

data_points.notable_features: Near-century-old building located in the Loop's main tourism area, already zoned for residential use.
data_points.project_notes: Building was marketed for redevelopment from office to multifamily. Contracts for most business tenants included landlord termination rights.

articles.market_intelligence: Office space in the Chicagoland area is being repurposed, leading to decreasing office vacancy rates in both downtown and the suburbs for the first time since the pandemic. In the suburbs, net absorption rate is up, and downtown buyers and owners are focusing on redevelopment to fill underutilized buildings. This conversion trend also stands to chip away at rents, which have increased amidst a construction pipeline drought.

articles.title: Sterling Bay plans to offload Fulton Market site to Range Group for 109-unit mid-rise project
articles.narrative: Range Group is under contract to acquire a 27,714-square-foot site in Chicago's Fulton Market from Sterling Bay, with plans to develop a 109-unit mid-rise apartment building. The proposed five-story project at 113 West Kinzie Street includes 15% affordable units, with a fee-in-lieu for the remaining 5% to meet the city's 20% affordability requirement. This development reflects a trend of smaller residential projects emerging in the resilient Fulton Market district.

data_points.notable_features: Proposed five-story mid-rise apartment building with 15% affordable units and a fee-in-lieu for the remaining 5% to meet city requirements.
data_points.project_notes: Site is one of three properties Sterling Bay is offloading for residential redevelopment.

articles.market_intelligence: Fulton Market has shown strong resilience to pandemic-era property value declines in downtown Chicago. Smaller residential projects are increasing in the district due to a slowed large-scale project pipeline and efforts to balance infrastructure strain with historic preservation. Average rents at a comparable Tishman Speyer building in the area are $3,133 per unit, with its 12,436-square-foot retail area fully leased.

articles.title: Is the suburban Chicago office exodus ending? Vacancy rates edge lower
articles.narrative: Suburban Chicago office vacancy rates have shown their first quarterly decrease since 2019, dropping from 33.4% to 33.1%. This positive shift is partly attributed to the redevelopment of obsolete office space, which has reduced the overall suburban office inventory from 100.5 million square feet to 93.2 million square feet. The market continues to see a 'flight to quality,' with trophy office properties experiencing the lowest vacancy rates and driving net absorption up by 32,000 square feet for the quarter.

articles.title: Fort Worth Stockyards will get $71M apartment project as $1B planned redevelopment hangs in balance

This project represents the residential component of a larger 14.6-acre mixed-use development, Stockyards North, which also plans for a hotel, retail, and dining options. The development aims to create a walkable and affordable district, marking Fort Worth Housing Solutions' initial venture into the area surrounding the historic district.

Prologis extends San Jose streak with $12M building buy

This acquisition adds to Prologis's significant holdings in the region, where it is the largest commercial property owner.

articles.title: San Jose’s deal for Urban Catalyst building faces pushback over resi goals
articles.narrative: A proposed 276-unit apartment project in downtown San Jose, known as The Gifford, is facing delays in its approval process due to neighborhood opposition regarding its design and compatibility with surrounding single-family homes. This development is linked to a separate agreement where the City of San Jose plans to acquire the historic Knox-Goodrich building from Urban Catalyst for $3.6 million, with the expectation that Urban Catalyst would then commence construction on The Gifford. Despite city officials asserting the independence of the two approvals, the intertwined nature of the deals has drawn additional scrutiny as the city aims to meet its state-mandated housing creation goals.

articles.title: Brookfield ups market-rate unit count, building heights at Pier 70 project
articles.narrative: Brookfield Properties is seeking to increase the residential unit count and building heights for its Pier 70 redevelopment in San Francisco's Dogpatch neighborhood. The proposed changes would raise the maximum residential count from 2,150 to 2,750 units and increase building heights from 70 feet to 90 feet. This adjustment aims to make the project more financially viable, allowing Brookfield to break ground on the first market-rate apartment building, a 350-unit project, in 2027. The overall first phase of development would now include 700 homes, up from 575 units, with the additional density helping the project pencil out amidst rising construction costs.

data_points.notable_features: Waterfront site in the Dogpatch neighborhood, with residential buildings proposed to reach 90 feet in height.
data_points.project_notes: The project's existing voter-approved framework from 2015 allows for a maximum height of 90 feet. The first development phase will consist of 700 homes, including a 350-unit market-rate apartment building. The proposal would reduce the percentage of affordable housing from 30% to 20% due to the increased overall unit count, though the total number of affordable units would remain unchanged. Building 12, a former shipbuilding structure within the project, has already been redeveloped for various commercial and recreational uses.

articles.title: Life Sciences Employers Consider Areas Beyond Established Biopharm Hubs
articles.narrative: A new report from Cushman & Wakefield indicates that while established life sciences hubs like Boston-Cambridge and the San Francisco Bay Area continue to dominate in R&D and pharmaceutical manufacturing employment, secondary markets are gaining competitiveness. The report highlights that employers are increasingly considering factors beyond traditional biotech clusters, such as the cost of living, which favors Midwest and Southeast markets offering more cost-efficient labor environments. Education pipelines are also a critical differentiator, with Texas markets like Austin, Dallas, and Houston showing significant growth in life-science related degree completions, strengthening their talent pools. Despite some hiring bumps in 2023-2025, life sciences employment has steadied in the first half of 2026, with a modest but notable shift towards earlier-career hires, though challenges remain in filling specialized roles in AI and data science.

articles.title: CRE Strategies Could Help Preserve Value in Life Sciences Mergers & Acquisitions
articles.narrative: A new CBRE report highlights how corporate real estate (CRE) strategies can help preserve value in life sciences mergers and acquisitions, particularly as pharmaceutical companies acquire sponsor-backed biotech firms. The report identifies "stranding" as a common issue where acquired biotechs, despite smaller footprints, remain only partially integrated, leading to fragmented systems and inconsistent reporting. CBRE estimates that preventable real estate-related risks could amount to approximately 1% of deal value across serial acquisitions, potentially exceeding $100 million over several years for large organizations. To mitigate this, the report recommends focusing on CRE integration rather than immediate consolidation, suggesting a playbook that includes documenting real estate operations within 90 days post-closing and conducting portfolio-wide reviews every 18-24 months to standardize processes and protect long-term value.

articles.title: Gale Associates to Lead Rehab of Mansfield Municipal Airport Runway
articles.narrative: Gale Associates, Inc. has been selected to provide engineering design and construction administration services for the rehabilitation of Mansfield Municipal Airport's primary airfield infrastructure. This project marks the first reconstruction of the airport's main runway since 1993 and will involve upgrading the runway, taxiways, drainage system, and airfield electrical infrastructure to meet current FAA standards. While fixed-wing operations will be temporarily suspended during the three-month construction period, Boston MedFlight will continue its emergency medical transport services from the airport.

data_points.notable_features: First reconstruction of the primary runway since 1993; Boston MedFlight will maintain operations during construction.
data_points.project_notes: Project includes reconstruction of Runway 14-32, Taxiway A, and connecting stub taxiways, along with Taxiways B, C, D edge lighting. Upgrades to drainage, airfield electrical infrastructure, guidance signs, runway and taxiway lighting, navigational aids, a new electrical vault, pavement markings, and site restoration are also part of the project.

articles.title: Capital Arrives in the Sunbelt for the Right Multifamily Deals
articles.narrative: Despite recent struggles in the Sunbelt multifamily market due to high unit deliveries, rising interest rates, and softening rent growth, investors are increasingly identifying opportunities in well-located properties with experienced sponsors and realistic underwriting. The market has become more disciplined, with a shift in focus from avoiding the region to strategically investing in specific submarkets and at appropriate price points. While capital is available for acquisitions and developments, it is subject to greater scrutiny, with lenders emphasizing submarket supply, lease-up assumptions, concessions, sponsor strength, and projected exit cap rates rather than aggressive rent growth projections. This conservative approach, coupled with a belief that the current supply imbalance will correct as new construction moderates and population growth continues, is leading patient investors to commit capital now for anticipated strong long-term performance.

articles.title: Industrial Rebound Fuels New Wave Of Speculative Projects
articles.narrative: The U.S. industrial market is experiencing a resurgence in speculative development, driven by tightening vacancy rates, increased logistics demand, and new federal incentives for domestic manufacturing. Major players like Prologis are significantly expanding their development pipelines, with the company breaking ground on more new projects in the first half of the year than in all of 2025. This renewed confidence is fueled by strong leasing activity, particularly for large blocks of space, and improving market fundamentals across numerous markets, despite ongoing economic and geopolitical uncertainties. Developers are increasingly comfortable initiating new projects, including later phases of previously paused pandemic-era developments, as tenant demand continues to absorb available space.

articles.market_intelligence: U.S. industrial market leasing dynamics are generally tilting back toward landlords, with large swaths of available space being steadily leased. Occupiers are inking deals despite the volatile economic and geopolitical landscape, including the U.S. war with Iran blocking the Strait of Hormuz. The 'One Big Beautiful Bill Act' passed in July 2025, providing tax and policy incentives to bring manufacturing back to the U.S., has injected certainty into developers' calculus and broadened the ecosystem of industrial occupiers.

articles.title: How One Firm Is Leaning Into A Growing Secondaries Market
articles.narrative: Partners Group, a UK-based firm, is actively leveraging the growing real estate secondaries market, having invested $6 billion across over 120 transactions since 2008. The firm is currently targeting a $1.5 billion fundraise for its fifth real estate secondaries program, which has already secured over $650 million in commitments. The secondaries market has evolved from a simple liquidity tool to a more strategic mechanism for managers to execute business plans and for investors to rebalance portfolios, especially in a market characterized by reduced distributions and slower fundraising cycles. Partners Group focuses on thematic investments, primarily targeting living and industrial asset classes, while largely avoiding office properties.
articles.market_intelligence: Global real estate secondaries transaction volume reached $25.1 billion in 2025, a 3% increase from $24.3 billion in 2024. GP-led secondaries constituted 64% of this volume at $16.1 billion, while LP-led secondaries totaled $8.8 billion, up 15% from the previous year. Industrial transactions led the market at $6.7 billion in 2025, followed by multifamily at $5 billion. Other living sectors, including student and senior housing, saw significant growth in transaction volumes, increasing by 67% and 92% respectively.

articles.title: Silicon Valley Cities See Spike In Office Demolitions
articles.narrative: A growing trend of office demolitions and conversions to multifamily housing is emerging across Silicon Valley cities like Sunnyvale, San Mateo, and Menlo Park. This shift is driven by state mandates for increased housing density, significant appreciation in apartment rents, and the obsolescence of many lower-tier office buildings. Developers are finding that razing outdated office structures to build new apartments, or converting well-suited office towers, is a more viable strategy than attempting to lease vacant office space, especially given the challenges of converting buildings with unfavorable layouts. The upzoning efforts by local municipalities, spurred by state housing requirements, are making these projects financially feasible by allowing for higher density and maximizing unit counts.

articles.title: With Bump In Defense Spending, Massachusetts Reaches For A Bigger Slice Of The Pie
articles.narrative: Massachusetts is actively pursuing a larger share of increased federal defense spending, leveraging its strong innovation economy, academic institutions, and existing defense contractor presence. The Healey-Driscoll administration launched the Strategic Hub for Innovation, Exchange and Leadership in Defense (SHIELD) to foster growth in the state's defense sector. This initiative aims to attract defense contractors expanding their real estate footprints, with recent examples including a proposed 1M SF manufacturing facility by VulcanForms in Devens and GE Aerospace's $42M investment in its Lynn manufacturing plant. The state's defense sector contributed $50B to the Massachusetts economy in fiscal year 2024, surpassing its life sciences sector, and officials are optimistic that continued federal investment will further boost the local economy.

articles.title: 1 In 10 NYC Cooling Tower Checks Find Legionella-Linked Violations
articles.narrative: A Bisnow analysis of New York City Health Department data reveals that 70% of cooling tower inspections since 2017 have resulted in violations, with nearly 10% of these being public health hazards directly linked to Legionella bacteria. This widespread non-compliance is complicating the city's response to a recent Legionnaires' disease outbreak in the Upper East Side, where 64 cases have been reported. Experts attribute the high rate of violations to factors like inadequate maintenance programs, failure to test for Legionella, or ignored elevated test results, creating ideal conditions for bacterial growth and dissemination. Despite increased regulations and fines following previous outbreaks, many building owners continue to fall short of compliance, highlighting a systemic issue where self-certification often lacks sufficient third-party oversight.

articles.market_intelligence: New York City first imposed cooling tower regulations in 2015 after a Legionnaires' outbreak in the South Bronx infected 138 people and killed 16. Regulations were increased in November last year following another outbreak in Harlem that infected 114 and killed seven. Current law requires building owners to test for Legionella every 31 days and clean towers twice a year. Fines for non-compliance have also been raised.
